description: Still Out There is an interactive STEM website by Team VU Aphelion (Varendra University) for NASA Space Apps 2026. Designed for kids aged 10-14, it brings NASA's abandoned machines on the Moon and Mars to life.
summary: Still Out There is an interactive website that lets NASA's abandoned machines tell their own stories to children aged 10 to 14. Students choose the Moon or Mars, tap a glowing marker, and meet a machine: the Apollo 11 Retroreflector, Surveyor 3, the Spirit rover or the InSight lander. Each machine speaks in the first person with real NASA images, and students explore how it worked by sending a laser to the Moon, tapping parts of the hardware, and following a timeline. A short Mission Check turns each story into a game, earning badges, mission progress and backpack items, guided by a friendly character named Orbit .The project addresses the challenge by turning dense mission data into an accurate, story-driven experience that shows how the hardware worked and what science it made possible. It matters because young people mostly hear about active missions, yet machines like Spirit, planned for 90 days and working for years, paved the way for today's exploration. All images are credited to NASA, and the project is not endorsed by NASA. Next, we plan to add more machines, Bangla language support, and a teacher mode.
details: WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS Still Out There is an interactive web experience for students aged 10 to 14. A child picks the Moon or Mars, taps a glowing marker, and meets a NASA machine left behind: the Apollo 11 Retroreflector, Surveyor 3, the Spirit rover or the InSight lander. Each machine tells its own story in the first person ("I was built to send light home"). Instead of only reading facts, students explore how the hardware worked: they send a laser to the Moon, tap parts of the machine to see what each did, and follow a short timeline. A three-question Mission Check ends each story. Progress, badges and a backpack of collected items keep children exploring, and a guide character named Orbit welcomes them. BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT Children usually hear only about active missions. Our project turns dense mission history into stories they remember, so these machines become characters, not dates. Students learn real science, such as how mirrors measure the Earth-Moon distance without any power, and why a rover built for 90 days can work for years. We plan to add more machines, Bangla language support so every child in Bangladesh can use it, and a teacher mode for classrooms. TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY A web application deployed on Vercel. [Add your stack here, e.g. languages, framework, libraries.] Images come from the NASA Image and Video Library and are credited on each page. Mission facts come from NASA sources. WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE The machines speak for themselves. Each one has its own voice and its own small interaction, and the story is told through play rather than a list of facts. FACTORS WE CONSIDERED Accuracy: facts are drawn from NASA sources and every image is credited. Age: simple language and short stories for ages 10 to 14. Accessibility: the story is available as text as well as narration, there is a light mode and a skip-to-content link, and sound can be turned off. Honesty: the project states clearly that it is not endorsed by NASA.
